title: Morrison v. Olson (1988)
summary: The Court upheld the independent counsel scheme, including judicial appointment and good-cause removal, while Scalia argued that prosecution had to remain under exclusive presidential control.
notes: Chief Justice Rehnquist wrote the 7-1 opinion; the Court also held that the Special Division's appointment powers did not violate Article III.

sections.Parties: Independent counsel Alexia Morrison investigated former Assistant Attorney General Theodore Olson. Olson and other subpoena recipients challenged the statutory arrangements; the Attorney General and the specially constituted judicial division played the appointment and oversight roles established by the Ethics in Government Act.
sections.Material Facts: After a conflict between the administration and congressional investigators over EPA documents, a House committee alleged that Olson had given false or misleading testimony. Attorney General Meese sought an independent counsel for Olson; the Special Division initially appointed McKay and then Morrison after McKay resigned. The Act limited the counsel to defined investigative and prosecutorial work, required adherence to Justice Department policy where possible, and allowed personal removal by the Attorney General only for good cause. The Attorney General controlled the initial decision to seek an appointment; the judicial division selected the counsel and defined jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: Olson and two other recipients moved to quash Morrison’s subpoenas. The D.C. Circuit invalidated the arrangement. The Supreme Court reversed that constitutional determination by a seven-to-one vote, with Kennedy recused and Scalia dissenting. The decision upheld the scheme; it did not adjudicate whether Olson had committed the investigated offense.
sections.Issue: Was the counsel an inferior officer whom a court could appoint, and did her removal protection and the scheme as a whole impermissibly impair executive authority?
sections.Holding: The counsel was an inferior officer; judicial appointment was permissible; the good-cause restriction and overall scheme did not impermissibly interfere with the President’s constitutional functions.
sections.Reasoning: The Court relied on limited duties, jurisdiction, and tenure and removability by a higher executive official to classify the counsel as inferior. The Appointments Clause allowed interbranch appointments subject to functional incompatibility limits; judges who appointed counsel could not adjudicate matters involving that counsel. On removal, the Court shifted emphasis from labels such as purely executive to whether the restriction impeded the President’s constitutional work. It found sufficient executive control through the Attorney General’s initiation decision, jurisdictional submission, good-cause removal, and Justice Department policies. Congress had not reserved removal or supervision for itself. Scalia regarded prosecution as executive power requiring exclusive presidential control and disputed both inferior status and the adequacy of the asserted safeguards. He also feared a single-investigation prosecutor would lack the competing responsibilities that normally discipline prosecutorial judgment. These competing constitutional approaches remain distinct in the assigned treatment.

topics.lrs-s-inferior-officer: Limited duties, jurisdiction, tenure, and removal by the Attorney General supported inferior status under the majority’s approach.
topics.lrs-s-removal: The majority asked whether good-cause protection impaired presidential functions rather than relying exclusively on formal power labels.
topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: Judicial appointment of an inferior prosecutor was permissible without an incongruity or impairment of judicial functions.
topics.lrs-s-congressional-control: Congress’s lack of a direct removal or supervisory role distinguished Myers and Bowsher.
topics.lrs-s-agency-independence: The good-cause removal holding is the doctrinal basis for insulating prosecutorial and agency officials from at-will removal.
topics.lrs-s-accountability: Scalia's dissent frames exclusive presidential control of prosecution as a matter of political accountability.
